title: Selective Laser Melting of Magnesium and Magnesium Alloy Powders: Materials, Process Fundamentals, Microstructure, Properties, and Applications

subsections.section_title: Introduction and Scope of Selective Laser Melting for Magnesium-Based Materials
subsections.subsection_title: Magnesium and magnesium alloys as advanced engineering materials
subsections.content:
Magnesium and its alloys occupy a distinctive position among engineering metals because of their exceptionally low density (~1.74 g cm^-3), high specific strength and stiffness, good castability, and useful electromagnetic shielding and damping characteristics. These attributes make Mg-based materials attractive wherever mass reduction is directly linked to energy efficiency or functional performance, notably in transportation, portable electronics, and biomedical devices. A broad overview of alloy classes, strengthening routes, and application drivers is provided in ref [1].

The engineering relevance of magnesium is further enhanced by the tunability of its microstructure through alloying with Al, Zn, Mn, rare earth elements, Zr, Ca, and others, enabling trade-offs among strength, ductility, creep resistance, ignition resistance, and corrosion behavior. At the same time, the hexagonal close-packed crystal structure limits the number of easy slip systems at ambient temperature, so conventional wrought processing often struggles to simultaneously achieve high strength and formability. Recent alloy design strategies therefore emphasize texture control, precipitation engineering, and solute effects to overcome these intrinsic deformation constraints, as discussed in ref [2].

For biomedical engineering, magnesium also offers a rare combination of mechanical compatibility with bone and intrinsic biodegradability, motivating interest in temporary implants and porous scaffolds. However, rapid corrosion and associated hydrogen evolution remain central barriers to broader use, requiring careful control of composition, impurity level, and microstructure ref [3]. These diverse opportunities and limitations explain why magnesium alloys are increasingly viewed as advanced, application-specific materials rather than merely lightweight substitutes for aluminum or steel.

subsections.section_title: Introduction and Scope of Selective Laser Melting for Magnesium-Based Materials
subsections.subsection_title: Why selective laser melting for magnesium
subsections.content:
Selective laser melting is especially attractive for magnesium because it links the metal’s low density and high specific properties with the geometric freedom of additive manufacturing. Conventional casting and wrought processing of magnesium alloys are often constrained by limited formability, segregation, and the difficulty of producing intricate lightweight architectures. By contrast, layer-wise melting enables near-net-shape fabrication of topology-optimized components, lattice structures, and patient-specific implants that would be difficult or uneconomical to manufacture otherwise. This design freedom is particularly relevant for biomedical and weight-critical engineering applications, where magnesium’s combination of low elastic modulus, biodegradability, or high specific stiffness can be exploited more fully through tailored porous or complex geometries ref [4], ref [5].

Beyond geometric complexity, SLM offers a distinctive microstructural advantage for magnesium alloys. The extremely high cooling rates associated with laser melting can refine grains, suppress coarse secondary phases, and extend solid solubility, thereby opening processing routes to microstructures that are difficult to obtain by equilibrium methods. Such nonequilibrium refinement is important because the mechanical behavior and corrosion response of magnesium are highly sensitive to grain size and phase distribution. In this sense, SLM is not merely a shaping technique, but also a microstructure-engineering tool that may enable improved strength, controlled degradation, and functional performance in alloys designed specifically for additive manufacturing ref [6], ref [7].

subsections.section_title: Introduction and Scope of Selective Laser Melting for Magnesium-Based Materials
subsections.subsection_title: Distinctive challenges in laser processing of magnesium powders
subsections.content:
Laser processing of magnesium powders is intrinsically difficult because the material combines high chemical reactivity with a comparatively low melting and boiling temperature range. Under the intense and highly localized energy input of SLM, magnesium readily oxidizes or even ignites if oxygen control is inadequate, while vaporization-induced recoil pressure can destabilize the melt pool. These effects narrow the usable process window and make defect suppression substantially more demanding than for less reactive structural alloys ref [8], ref [9].

A second challenge arises from the thermophysical characteristics of magnesium melts and powders. Low viscosity, high vapor pressure, and rapid heat extraction promote balling, spatter, denudation of surrounding powder, and lack-of-fusion/porosity when volumetric energy density is not carefully balanced. Because evaporation changes local composition and intensifies plume formation, process parameters cannot be transferred straightforwardly from aluminum, titanium, or steels; scan strategy, layer thickness, and shielding atmosphere must be tailored specifically for Mg-based systems ref [9], ref [10].

These processing instabilities are coupled to microstructural and property-related risks. Oxide contamination and keyhole or gas porosity can impair corrosion behavior, fatigue resistance, and ductility, which is particularly critical for biodegradable and lightweight structural applications. Consequently, successful SLM of magnesium requires simultaneous control of powder quality, atmosphere purity, laser energy input, and thermal history rather than simple densification optimization alone ref [8], ref [10].

subsections.section_title: Introduction and Scope of Selective Laser Melting for Magnesium-Based Materials
subsections.subsection_title: Historical development and current research landscape
subsections.content:
Research on laser powder bed fusion of magnesium emerged later than analogous work on steels, Ti, and Al because Mg combines a narrow processing window with high vapor pressure, strong oxidation tendency, and flammability. A recognizable early milestone was the demonstration that dense Mg-rich parts could be fabricated by selective laser melting and that process parameters strongly controlled porosity, grain refinement, and strength, as shown for Mg–9Al powders in one of the first detailed experimental studies in this area ref [6].

Subsequent work broadened from proof-of-concept fabrication toward alloy-specific optimization and application-driven design. Studies on WE43 established the feasibility of producing rare-earth-containing magnesium alloys with refined microstructures and competitive mechanical response by selective laser melting, while also clarifying the roles of energy density, evaporation losses, and cracking susceptibility ref [11]. In parallel, biomedical interest accelerated the field because additive manufacturing offers patient-specific porous architectures for biodegradable implants, linking process science to corrosion and biocompatibility requirements ref [5].

The current research landscape is therefore characterized by three converging directions: process-window stabilization for reactive powders, composition and feedstock design to suppress evaporation and defect formation, and structure-property-performance studies spanning mechanical behavior, corrosion, and degradation. More recent investigations increasingly integrate in situ process monitoring, tailored scan strategies, and post-processing routes, indicating a transition from exploratory feasibility studies to more application-oriented and mechanism-informed development.

subsections.section_title: Introduction and Scope of Selective Laser Melting for Magnesium-Based Materials
subsections.subsection_title: Objectives and structure of the survey
subsections.content:
This survey aims to consolidate the rapidly expanding but still fragmented literature on selective laser melting (SLM) of magnesium-based powders, with emphasis on the interdependence of powder characteristics, process physics, defect formation, microstructure evolution, mechanical performance, corrosion behavior, and application-specific requirements. In contrast to broader overviews of additive manufacturing for biodegradable or lightweight metals, the present survey focuses specifically on the scientific issues that arise from magnesium’s high chemical reactivity, low boiling temperature, and narrow processing window under laser irradiation ref [8], ref [4].

A second objective is to identify unifying process–structure–property relationships across pure Mg and representative alloy systems, including rare-earth-containing, Al-containing, Zn-containing, Ca-containing, and biomedical compositions. Particular attention is given to how energy density, scan strategy, atmosphere control, and feedstock condition influence evaporation, spatter, porosity, cracking susceptibility, texture development, and anisotropy, as well as how these features govern tensile response, fatigue resistance, degradation behavior, and biocompatibility in service ref [12].

Accordingly, the survey is structured to move from materials background and process-specific challenges to detailed discussions of powder design, parameter optimization, microstructural control, post-processing, functional performance, and emerging applications. The final sections synthesize unresolved scientific questions and translational barriers, highlighting priorities for future research such as in situ monitoring, composition design for printability, and standardized evaluation protocols for structural and biomedical uses ref [9].

subsections.section_title: Powder Feedstock Design and Materials Selection for SLM of Magnesium and Magnesium Alloys
subsections.subsection_title: Powder production routes and feedstock quality
subsections.content:
Powder production route is a primary determinant of SLM processability because it controls particle size distribution, morphology, internal porosity, and flow behavior. For magnesium alloys, gas atomization is generally preferred over mechanically milled or irregular powders because it produces more spherical particles with better spreadability and more stable layer deposition, which is especially important for a low-density, highly reactive metal. Studies on SLM of magnesium alloys commonly attribute improved densification and reduced lack-of-fusion defects to powders with high sphericity, limited satellites, and a narrow size fraction suited to the recoating system and laser spot size ref [11], ref [6].

Feedstock quality requirements for magnesium are therefore stringent: particles should exhibit low oxygen pickup, minimal entrapped gas, and consistent chemistry from particle to particle. In practice, excessively fine powders can aggravate oxidation risk and powder-bed disturbance, whereas overly coarse powders reduce packing density and melt-track continuity. Investigations on WE43 and related Mg alloys processed by SLM show that feedstock characteristics strongly interact with volumetric energy density to determine pore formation, evaporation behavior, and final microstructure ref [10].

Beyond morphology, compositional homogeneity inherited from atomization is also important because segregation or oxide-rich particle surfaces can destabilize melting and solidification. Consequently, powder qualification for SLM magnesium should include not only size and shape analysis, but also measurements of flowability, apparent density, oxygen content, and reuse-induced degradation. Such controls are essential for translating laboratory printability into reproducible part quality.

subsections.section_title: Powder Feedstock Design and Materials Selection for SLM of Magnesium and Magnesium Alloys
subsections.subsection_title: Surface chemistry, oxidation, and storage of magnesium powders
subsections.content:
Surface chemistry is unusually important for SLM of magnesium powders because of magnesium’s high affinity for oxygen and moisture. Even when atomized powders appear metallic, they are typically covered by a thin native MgO/Mg(OH)2-containing surface film that strongly influences laser absorptivity, inter-particle contact, wetting, and melt pool stability. More critically, oxidation of fine particles increases the risk of spatter, smoke generation, and powder ignition during handling and processing, so surface condition becomes a central part of feedstock qualification rather than a secondary storage issue ref [13], ref [14].

The oxide film is not necessarily detrimental in all cases: a thin, uniform layer can passivate the powder and reduce catastrophic oxidation, but thickened or chemically heterogeneous films promote lack-of-fusion defects, entrapped oxides, and inconsistent remelting behavior. For magnesium, this balance is especially delicate because oxidation kinetics are rapid and strongly accelerated by humidity; exposure to air can convert surface MgO toward hydroxylated products, which modifies flowability and can introduce hydrogen-bearing species relevant to porosity formation during melting ref [14], ref [15].

Accordingly, storage protocols for Mg feedstocks are stricter than for many Al or Ti powders. Low-humidity inert atmospheres, sealed containers, minimized thermal cycling, and limited residence time outside glovebox or dry-room conditions are commonly required. Powder reuse must also be monitored through oxygen pickup, changes in particle surface chemistry, and the accumulation of partially oxidized fines, since these changes can progressively narrow the safe processing window and reduce part quality ref [13], ref [16].

subsections.section_title: Powder Feedstock Design and Materials Selection for SLM of Magnesium and Magnesium Alloys
subsections.subsection_title: Pure magnesium versus alloyed magnesium powders
subsections.content:
From a feedstock-selection perspective, pure Mg offers the clearest compositional baseline for studying melt-track stability, densification, and biodegradation response, but it is generally the most difficult option to process robustly by SLM. Its narrow processing window is associated with high vapor pressure, strong laser absorptivity changes during melting, and the absence of alloying elements that can widen solidification ranges or promote beneficial grain refinement. Studies on SLM of pure magnesium therefore commonly report a stronger sensitivity to energy density and shielding conditions than is typical for established Mg alloys ref [17].

Alloyed powders are usually favored because composition can be used as a process-design variable. In conventional casting alloys such as AZ- and ZK-type systems, Al, Zn, Zr, and rare-earth additions modify melting behavior, strengthen the solid solution or precipitate population, and can reduce hot-cracking susceptibility through microstructural refinement. In particular, WE43 has become a prominent benchmark feedstock in powder-bed fusion because it combines comparatively good printability with high as-built strength and a refined cellular or equiaxed microstructure under rapid solidification ref [11].

The trade-off is that alloying also introduces application-specific constraints. For biodegradable implants, pure Mg is attractive because it avoids potential biological concerns linked to some alloying additions, whereas structural or high-performance biomedical applications often require alloyed powders to achieve sufficient strength, creep resistance, or corrosion control. Accordingly, powder selection is not simply a comparison between pure and alloyed Mg, but a balance among processability, defect tolerance, target microstructure, and service environment ref [3], ref [2].

subsections.section_title: Powder Feedstock Design and Materials Selection for SLM of Magnesium and Magnesium Alloys
subsections.subsection_title: Conventional magnesium alloy systems for additive manufacturing
subsections.content:
Among conventional magnesium alloy families explored for SLM, Al-containing cast alloys and rare-earth-containing wrought/cast alloys have received the most attention because they offer markedly different processing windows and property profiles. Early work on AZ-type compositions showed that Mg–Al alloys can be processed to near-dense parts, but their high vapor pressure, oxidation sensitivity, and tendency toward evaporation-induced composition shifts demand tight control of laser energy density and shielding quality. In parallel, rare-earth-bearing systems such as WE43 emerged as especially attractive because their solidification behavior, precipitation response, and good biocompatibility made them suitable for both lightweight structural and biodegradable implant applications ref [6], ref [5].

AZ91 and related Mg–Al–Zn alloys remain important benchmark systems because they are commercially available, relatively well understood, and useful for isolating the effects of scan strategy and heat input on porosity, grain refinement, and cracking behavior. However, their broad freezing range and susceptibility to Mg evaporation can compromise dimensional stability and compositional fidelity during processing. By contrast, WE43 has become the de facto reference alloy for magnesium LPBF/SLM, with studies reporting fine cellular-to-equiaxed microstructures, high strength in the as-built state, and substantial sensitivity to process-induced evaporation of Mg and redistribution of rare-earth elements ref [11].

From a materials-selection perspective, these conventional systems illustrate the central trade-off in magnesium AM: widely used industrial alloys provide a practical starting point, but were not originally designed for rapid laser melting and solidification. Consequently, conventional AZ-, ZK-, and WE-type powders are valuable baseline feedstocks, yet they also motivate the alloy redesign strategies discussed in the following subsection ref [5], ref [1].

subsections.section_title: Powder Feedstock Design and Materials Selection for SLM of Magnesium and Magnesium Alloys
subsections.subsection_title: Alloy design strategies for improved printability and performance
subsections.content:
Alloy design for SLM of magnesium must balance a narrow processing window, high vapor pressure, and strong oxidation tendency against the need for adequate densification and property retention. A central strategy is to introduce alloying elements that widen the freezing range only modestly while promoting constitutional undercooling and grain refinement, thereby reducing hot cracking and improving melt-track stability. Rare-earth-containing systems such as WE-type alloys are attractive in this respect because they combine comparatively good laser processability with fine equiaxed microstructures and useful age-hardening potential after fabrication ref [11].

A second strategy is to tailor composition toward in situ grain-refining and texture-weakening effects. Solutes such as Zr and selected rare earths can increase heterogeneous nucleation and suppress the strong basal texture often associated with magnesium solidification, which helps improve both isotropy and crack resistance. More broadly, high-strength magnesium alloy development has shown that alloy chemistries based on rare earths, Zn, Ca, and Zr can simultaneously refine grains, stabilize precipitate populations, and improve elevated-temperature response; these principles are directly relevant when adapting compositions for the rapid solidification conditions of SLM ref [2].

For biomedical SLM applications, alloy design must additionally consider corrosion and biocompatibility. This has motivated growing interest in Ca-, Zn-, and rare-earth-lean compositions that avoid excessive Al while still improving printability relative to pure Mg. Recent reviews of laser additive manufacturing of magnesium alloys therefore emphasize composition design as a process-enabling tool rather than a purely performance-driven choice: optimized chemistry can reduce evaporation-induced defects, improve powder-bed fusion consistency, and create microstructures better suited to post-build heat treatment and service requirements ref [12], ref [8].

subsections.section_title: Powder Feedstock Design and Materials Selection for SLM of Magnesium and Magnesium Alloys
subsections.subsection_title: Powder recyclability and reuse
subsections.content:
Powder recyclability is especially critical for SLM of magnesium because economic incentives for reuse are counterbalanced by the metal’s high chemical reactivity. In contrast to less reactive alloys, repeated handling, sieving, and exposure to the build chamber atmosphere can accelerate oxygen pickup, alter surface films, and increase the likelihood of moisture-related contamination. A broader LPBF literature has therefore emphasized that reused powders must be evaluated not only for particle size and flowability, but also for chemistry, morphology, and safety-related changes during storage and recirculation ref [16].

For magnesium feedstocks, the main concern is that reuse may progressively thicken or modify the native oxide/hydroxide layer, which can reduce absorptivity consistency, impair melt coalescence, and promote lack-of-fusion defects or inclusions. Because magnesium oxidation kinetics are strongly affected by temperature, humidity, and defect structure in the surface film, even small deviations in powder handling practice can have disproportionate effects on process stability ref [14]. This issue is particularly important for fine fractions, which possess higher specific surface area and are more susceptible to oxidation and ignition hazards ref [13].

Accordingly, reuse strategies for Mg powders should be conservative: controlled inert-atmosphere recovery, removal of spatter and condensate, periodic screening of particle size distribution and oxygen content, and clear limits on the number of recycle loops. At present, systematic reuse datasets for Mg alloy powders remain scarce, so qualification protocols are still largely inferred from general LPBF powder-management practice rather than from magnesium-specific lifecycle studies ref [16], ref [9].

subsections.section_title: Process Physics, SLM Parameters, and Manufacturing Challenges
subsections.subsection_title: Laser-powder interaction and energy absorption
subsections.content:
Laser–powder interaction in magnesium LPBF/SLM is dominated by the intrinsically high optical reflectivity and low boiling temperature of Mg, which together narrow the useful energy-input range. Relative to many engineering alloys, magnesium powders absorb a smaller fraction of incident near-infrared laser energy at room temperature, so efficient melting often depends on multiple scattering within the powder bed, local oxidation state, and the progressive increase in absorptivity as particles heat and begin to melt ref [17], ref [4]. As a result, the effective coupling of laser energy is not a fixed material constant but a transient powder-bed property shaped by particle size distribution, packing density, and surface condition.

This sensitivity is amplified by the large specific surface area of fine Mg powders. Thin oxide films can modify optical response and partially stabilize particles prior to melting, but they also introduce heterogeneity in absorptivity from particle to particle. Once melting initiates, the transition from discrete particles to a continuous liquid track markedly changes energy coupling; however, excessive local energy density can rapidly promote evaporation, recoil effects, and spatter because magnesium has a comparatively low latent barrier to vaporization ref [4], ref [12]. Consequently, parameter selection for Mg must balance the need to overcome poor initial absorptivity against the risk of unstable vapor-driven melt-pool behavior.

From a process-design perspective, this means that scan strategies and laser settings cannot be interpreted only through nominal volumetric energy density. The same nominal energy input may produce different thermal outcomes depending on hatch overlap, layer thickness, spot size, and powder morphology, all of which alter the spatial distribution of absorbed energy in the bed. For magnesium, robust processing therefore requires explicit attention to absorptivity evolution and powder-state effects, rather than assuming the laser-material coupling behavior established for denser, less volatile alloys ref [17], ref [10].

subsections.section_title: Process Physics, SLM Parameters, and Manufacturing Challenges
subsections.subsection_title: Melt pool dynamics and thermal behavior
subsections.content:
Melt pool behavior in SLM of magnesium is governed by the metal’s low boiling point, high vapor pressure, high thermal conductivity, and strong surface reactivity. These attributes promote intense evaporation and recoil pressure under localized laser heating, making the melt pool comparatively shallow, unstable, and highly sensitive to small changes in volumetric energy density. As a result, magnesium processing often operates close to the boundary between insufficient fusion and excessive vaporization, with melt track continuity strongly affected by wetting, capillarity, and transient denudation of surrounding powder ref [17], ref [12].

Thermally, the very high cooling rates characteristic of laser powder bed fusion produce steep thermal gradients and rapid solidification, which can refine grains but also intensify residual stress development and interlayer thermal mismatch. In magnesium alloys, repeated reheating from subsequent scan passes and layers further modifies solidification morphology, solute redistribution, and texture evolution, so the final microstructure reflects not only peak melt pool temperature but also the cumulative thermal history. Numerical and experimental studies on LPBF melt pools have shown that conduction-mode melting, Marangoni-driven flow, and recoil-pressure-induced depression can coexist over narrow parameter ranges, helping explain the abrupt transition from stable tracks to balling, lack-of-fusion, or keyhole-related porosity when process conditions shift slightly ref [12], ref [18].

For magnesium specifically, these dynamics imply that scan strategy and heat accumulation control are as important as nominal laser power and speed. Short scan vectors, moderated overlap, and parameter sets that suppress excessive peak temperatures are generally favored to stabilize the melt pool while preserving sufficient remelting for metallurgical bonding ref [17], ref [9].

subsections.section_title: Process Physics, SLM Parameters, and Manufacturing Challenges
subsections.subsection_title: Key process parameters and process windows
subsections.content:
For magnesium powder bed fusion, the practical process window is narrower than for many structural alloys because high reflectivity, low boiling temperature, and strong oxidation tendency amplify the sensitivity to laser power, scan speed, hatch spacing, layer thickness, and spot size. In consequence, volumetric energy density is often used only as a first-order guide: insufficient input promotes lack-of-fusion and interlayer discontinuities, whereas excessive input intensifies evaporation, recoil-pressure-driven instability, spatter, and balling. Experimental studies on pure Mg and WE43 consistently show that dense builds are obtained only within a restricted combination of moderate power and sufficiently high but not excessive scanning velocity, rather than by maximizing nominal energy input alone ref [17], ref [11].

A key point is that identical energy-density values can correspond to very different thermal histories. For magnesium, scan speed and layer thickness strongly affect melt pool lifetime and cooling rate, while hatch spacing and overlap govern remelting uniformity and pore closure. Thus, parameter optimization should be based on coupled criteria such as relative density, surface integrity, dimensional stability, and crack/pore suppression, not on a single scalar metric. Reviews of SLM processing of Mg alloys emphasize that alloy-specific absorptivity, powder morphology, and vaporization behavior shift the window substantially between compositions such as pure Mg, AZ-series alloys, and WE43 ref [4], ref [8].

Accordingly, robust process windows for magnesium are best described as multidimensional maps linking power-speed combinations with layer thickness, hatch distance, scan strategy, and preheating condition. This perspective is particularly important for translating laboratory parameter sets to larger parts, where heat accumulation and geometric effects can move the local process state outside the nominally optimized window.

subsections.section_title: Process Physics, SLM Parameters, and Manufacturing Challenges
subsections.subsection_title: Build atmosphere and safety considerations
subsections.content:
Build-atmosphere control is unusually critical in laser powder bed fusion of magnesium because Mg exhibits high oxygen affinity, rapid oxidation kinetics, and a relatively low ignition threshold in finely divided form. Consequently, inert-gas processing is not only a metallurgical requirement but also a primary safety barrier. In practice, argon is generally preferred over nitrogen because it minimizes chemical reactivity and helps suppress exothermic oxidation of entrained spatter or condensate; low residual oxygen and moisture are likewise essential to reduce oxide-film growth on powder particles and melt tracks, which otherwise degrades wetting and promotes lack-of-fusion defects ref [14], ref [16].

Safety considerations extend beyond the chamber atmosphere itself to the full powder-handling chain. Magnesium powder is combustible, and the hazard increases strongly with decreasing particle size and increasing surface area; powder dispersion, filter loading, and post-build powder recovery therefore require strict ignition-source control and dedicated fire-response protocols, since conventional extinguishing approaches are often ineffective for burning Mg ref [13]. During processing, vaporization and spatter can also generate fine condensate and deposit reactive material in the gas-circulation path, making robust gas-flow design, oxygen monitoring, and regular cleaning indispensable for stable operation.

Atmosphere quality additionally affects process consistency. Oxidized or partially hydrated powder surfaces alter laser absorptivity and melt-pool behavior, while recirculated powder may accumulate oxide contamination during repeated handling and exposure. For magnesium alloys, this links atmosphere management directly to powder recyclability, defect suppression, and reproducible part quality, reinforcing the need for tightly controlled inerting, sealed storage, and traceable powder reuse protocols ref [16], ref [12].

subsections.section_title: Process Physics, SLM Parameters, and Manufacturing Challenges
subsections.subsection_title: Defect formation mechanisms
subsections.content:
Defect formation in SLM of magnesium is dominated by the narrow processing window created by high reflectivity, low boiling temperature, and strong oxidation tendency. Insufficient volumetric energy density promotes lack-of-fusion defects, where partially melted particles and weak inter-track/inter-layer bonding leave irregular pores and crack-like voids. At the opposite extreme, excessive energy input intensifies evaporation and recoil pressure, destabilizing the melt pool and encouraging keyhole-type porosity, spatter generation, and surface denudation; these mechanisms have been reported in both pure Mg and Mg alloy builds ref [17], ref [6].

Thermal stresses provide a second major route to defect formation. Magnesium alloys often solidify rapidly under steep thermal gradients, so constrained shrinkage between adjacent scan tracks and layers can generate hot tearing or microcracking, especially in compositions with wide solidification ranges or segregation-prone interdendritic liquid. Oxide films and entrained particles can further act as crack initiators or inhibit metallurgical bonding. In WE43, for example, processing-dependent porosity and cracking have been linked to scan strategy and energy density through their control of melt pool continuity and residual stress accumulation ref [11].

Balling is another characteristic instability, arising when the melt track breaks into discontinuous droplets because of high surface tension, insufficient wetting, or unfavorable scan speed–power combinations. This defect degrades surface quality and creates precursors for subsequent lack-of-fusion pores. More broadly, reviews of magnesium powder-bed fusion emphasize that porosity, cracking, oxidation-related inclusions, and dimensional distortion are strongly coupled outcomes of melt pool instability and atmosphere sensitivity rather than isolated defects ref [4].

subsections.section_title: Process Physics, SLM Parameters, and Manufacturing Challenges
subsections.subsection_title: In situ monitoring and process control
subsections.content:
In situ monitoring is particularly valuable in laser powder bed fusion of magnesium because the process window is narrow and deviations can rapidly trigger spatter, unstable melt tracks, excessive evaporation, or even ignition-related hazards. Although magnesium-specific monitoring studies remain limited, the sensor modalities established for metal PBF are directly relevant: coaxial photodiodes and high-speed cameras capture melt-pool emission and plume intensity, while layerwise imaging reveals recoater streaks, powder-bed nonuniformity, and defect-prone regions. These signatures can be correlated with lack-of-fusion, keyholing, and balling phenomena, enabling anomaly detection during the build rather than only after ex situ inspection ref [19], ref [20].

For process control, the main opportunity is to couple optical signals to adaptive adjustment of laser power, scan speed, or hatch strategy so that melt-pool dimensions and thermal emission remain within acceptable bounds. Melt-pool monitoring has already been shown in metal additive manufacturing to provide statistically meaningful indicators of porosity formation and track instability, supporting closed-loop or supervisory control architectures ref [20], ref [21]. In magnesium, such approaches are especially attractive because they could compensate for local changes in absorptivity and powder packing while also warning against vaporization-driven excursions.

A practical challenge is that magnesium’s high reflectivity, low boiling temperature, and intense vapor/plume activity can distort optical measurements and reduce the robustness of signal interpretation. Consequently, reliable process control will likely require multimodal sensing combined with data-driven classification and physics-informed thresholds, rather than reliance on a single intensity metric. Broader metal AM reviews emphasize that integrating monitoring, defect prediction, and feedback control is becoming central to qualification of safety-critical builds, and this need is even more acute for reactive alloys such as magnesium ref [21], ref [22].

subsections.section_title: Process Physics, SLM Parameters, and Manufacturing Challenges
subsections.subsection_title: Numerical modeling and simulation of SLM for magnesium
subsections.content:
Numerical modeling of SLM for magnesium remains less mature than for Ti- or Ni-based systems, but it is especially important because Mg combines low boiling temperature, high vapor pressure, strong oxidation tendency, and rapid heat extraction, all of which narrow the stable processing window. Accordingly, most simulations adapt the broader laser powder bed fusion framework—transient heat transfer, melt-pool fluid flow, and phase-change formulations—to predict track geometry, cooling rate, and defect susceptibility under magnesium-specific thermophysical constraints ref [12], ref [23].

At the mesoscale, thermal and thermo-fluid models are used to relate laser power, scan speed, hatch spacing, and layer thickness to melt-pool dimensions and solidification conditions. For magnesium alloys, these predictions are particularly relevant because evaporation-induced recoil pressure, Marangoni convection, and unstable keyhole or depression behavior can strongly perturb the melt pool and promote balling, lack-of-fusion, or porosity. Reviews on metal AM modeling emphasize that incorporating temperature-dependent properties, latent heat, free-surface effects, and vaporization is essential for physically meaningful predictions, although these features are still simplified in many practical LPBF simulations ref [23], ref [18].

At larger scales, layer- and part-scale simulations are valuable for estimating thermal accumulation, residual stress, and distortion, which can be severe in thin-walled magnesium components because of steep thermal gradients and limited ductility. However, the predictive capability for Mg-specific SLM is still constrained by scarce high-temperature property data and limited validation against in situ measurements. Future progress will depend on coupling multi-scale models with calibrated evaporation/oxidation sub-models and process-monitoring data, so that simulation can move from qualitative process interpretation toward robust process-window optimization for magnesium powders ref [12], ref [18], ref [24].

subsections.section_title: Microstructure Evolution and Phase Development in SLM-Processed Magnesium Alloys
subsections.subsection_title: Rapid solidification and non-equilibrium microstructures
subsections.content:
Rapid solidification is a defining feature of SLM-processed Mg alloys because the melt pool experiences extremely steep thermal gradients and short solidification times. These conditions generally suppress diffusional equilibration, refine the cellular/dendritic scale, and extend solid solubility beyond equilibrium limits, so the as-built microstructure often differs markedly from that predicted by conventional casting phase diagrams. In early studies on SLM of pure Mg and Mg-based alloys, the resulting microstructures were consistently much finer than cast counterparts, with submicron to few-micron structural features attributed to the high cooling rates inherent to layerwise laser processing ref [17], ref [6].

For alloyed systems, non-equilibrium solidification also promotes elemental partitioning on very short length scales and the retention of metastable or supersaturated matrices. In SLM-built WE43, for example, the rapid thermal cycle was associated with a fine α-Mg matrix and a markedly modified distribution of rare-earth-containing secondary phases relative to conventionally processed material, indicating incomplete equilibrium phase selection during solidification and repeated reheating ref [11]. Comparable behavior has been reported in SLM Mg-Al alloys, where rapid solidification produced refined microstructures and altered β-phase development compared with slower-cooled routes ref [25].

These non-equilibrium features are important because they provide the starting state for subsequent thermal exposure during the build and for post-processing. The as-built supersaturated matrix, refined segregation pattern, and metastable intermetallic population can either enhance strength directly or act as precursors for later precipitation, coarsening, and homogenization, thereby linking SLM thermal history to the downstream evolution of texture, defects, and mechanical or corrosion performance.

subsections.section_title: Microstructure Evolution and Phase Development in SLM-Processed Magnesium Alloys
subsections.subsection_title: Grain morphology, crystallographic texture, and anisotropy
subsections.content:
In SLM-processed Mg alloys, grain morphology is governed by the steep thermal gradient, high solidification rate, and repeated remelting associated with overlapping scan tracks and successive layers. These conditions commonly produce very fine cellular or equiaxed grains within melt pools, but columnar growth can still emerge locally when the thermal gradient is strongly aligned with the build direction. For Mg alloys this competition is especially important because the hcp lattice offers fewer easy slip systems at room temperature, making grain size and shape unusually influential on strength and ductility. Studies on LPBF/SLM WE43 have shown that rapid solidification can suppress coarse cast-like grains and generate a refined microstructure with clear melt-pool-scale heterogeneity, while subsequent thermal cycling modifies the as-solidified grain network and local boundary character ref [11], ref [26].

Texture development in additively manufactured Mg is likewise process-sensitive. Because the preferred growth direction and epitaxial inheritance vary with scan strategy, laser energy density, and remelting history, the basal texture typical of wrought Mg can be weakened, rotated, or spatially fragmented in SLM builds. This is technologically significant: a strong alignment of basal planes relative to the loading axis promotes anisotropic yielding and tension-compression asymmetry, whereas texture weakening can improve more isotropic deformation. Texture control through path planning is therefore not merely a microstructural issue but a route to mitigating the intrinsic plastic anisotropy of hcp Mg alloys, consistent with broader understanding of texture-property relations in magnesium ref [27], ref [28].

subsections.section_title: Microstructure Evolution and Phase Development in SLM-Processed Magnesium Alloys
subsections.subsection_title: Precipitation, intermetallic formation, and solute redistribution
subsections.content:
The steep thermal gradients and repeated reheating inherent to SLM strongly suppress equilibrium precipitation while promoting solute trapping and nanoscale chemical heterogeneity. In Mg alloys this commonly yields supersaturated α-Mg cells or dendrites decorated by solute-enriched intercellular regions, with second phases forming only where local segregation and cyclic thermal exposure are sufficient to overcome kinetic barriers. For Al-containing compositions, rapid solidification can refine or partially suppress the coarse Mg17Al12 network typical of cast material, whereas subsequent layer-by-layer remelting may re-precipitate fine interdendritic particles and metastable intermetallic distributions that differ markedly from equilibrium solidification products ref [6], ref [25].

In rare-earth-containing systems such as WE43, SLM similarly drives non-equilibrium solute redistribution at melt-pool and cellular scales. Y- and Nd-rich boundary regions, nanoscale precipitates, and retained supersaturation have been reported, reflecting both high cooling rates and repeated sub-solidus thermal cycling during build. These features are important because they couple directly to strength and corrosion behavior: fine RE-containing particles can contribute to strengthening, but chemical partitioning and intermetallic continuity may also establish local galvanic contrasts. Post-build heat treatment therefore becomes a key lever for transforming the as-built segregated structure into a more stable precipitate population through dissolution, redistribution, and re-precipitation of strengthening phases ref [11], ref [2].

subsections.section_title: Microstructure Evolution and Phase Development in SLM-Processed Magnesium Alloys
subsections.subsection_title: Evaporation-induced compositional changes
subsections.content:
Evaporation is a particularly important compositional perturbation in SLM of magnesium alloys because Mg has a low boiling point and high vapor pressure relative to many common alloying additions. Under the steep thermal gradients and repeated remelting cycles characteristic of laser powder bed fusion, this volatility can drive preferential loss of Mg and, in multicomponent systems, differential evaporation of low-boiling elements such as Zn, thereby shifting local and bulk chemistry away from the nominal powder composition. These changes are amplified at high volumetric energy density, where keyhole-like depression, recoil pressure, and spatter ejection increase mass loss and compositional instability ref [18], ref [16].

For Mg alloys, evaporation-induced chemistry shifts alter both phase selection and corrosion/mechanical response. A reduction in Mg content can enrich rare-earth- or Al-containing residual liquid, modify eutectic fractions, and promote nonuniform intermetallic distribution after rapid solidification; conversely, loss of volatile solutes can suppress strengthening precipitate precursors. In biodegradable alloys, even modest Zn depletion is relevant because it changes both solid-solution strengthening and galvanic coupling between matrix and secondary phases. Process maps developed for magnesium LPBF therefore commonly emphasize a narrow energy-input window that balances densification against elemental burn-off and oxidation-related mass loss ref [10], ref [12].

From a microstructural perspective, evaporation is coupled to denudation, pore formation, and surface roughening, so compositional changes should not be treated independently from defect evolution. Practical mitigation strategies include lowering peak energy density, shortening interaction time, using high-purity inert atmospheres with stringent oxygen control, and selecting alloy chemistries less susceptible to selective vaporization. Quantitative composition verification of both built parts and recycled powder is consequently essential when interpreting phase constitution and comparing nominally identical SLM-processed magnesium alloys ref [16], ref [12].

subsections.section_title: Microstructure Evolution and Phase Development in SLM-Processed Magnesium Alloys
subsections.subsection_title: Residual stress and defect-microstructure interactions
subsections.content:
Residual stresses in SLM-processed Mg alloys arise from the exceptionally steep thermal gradients and repeated reheating inherent to layerwise melting. In magnesium, these stresses are especially consequential because the hexagonal crystal structure provides limited easy slip at ambient temperature, so thermal contraction can be accommodated heterogeneously through twinning, local plasticity, and strain concentration at melt-pool boundaries. More broadly, residual-stress development in metal additive manufacturing is strongly coupled to scan strategy, part geometry, and restraint conditions, and can therefore vary substantially even when porosity appears low ref [24].

Defects interact directly with this residual-stress field. Lack-of-fusion pores, keyhole voids, and partially fused particle clusters act as local stress concentrators that promote microcrack initiation, while cellular/columnar substructures and segregation bands can either impede or channel crack propagation depending on their orientation relative to the thermal history. For Mg alloys, where evaporation, oxide entrainment, and hot-tearing susceptibility are persistent concerns, this coupling between defect population and residual stress is a major determinant of tensile anisotropy, fatigue sensitivity, and corrosion-assisted damage initiation. Process optimization that reduces energy-density extremes and stabilizes melt-pool geometry is therefore important not only for densification but also for controlling stress-defect interactions ref [17], ref [10].

Post-build stress relief or hot isostatic pressing can reduce stored elastic strain and partially heal internal defects, but these treatments also modify the as-built microstructure through recovery, recrystallization, and precipitate evolution. Consequently, the net benefit depends on balancing crack-driving residual stress against the retention of fine rapidly solidified features that contribute to strength. Integrated experimental and modeling studies in additive manufacturing increasingly emphasize this process-structure-stress coupling as a prerequisite for reliable qualification of lightweight Mg components ref [24], ref [23].

subsections.section_title: Microstructure Evolution and Phase Development in SLM-Processed Magnesium Alloys
subsections.subsection_title: Effects of heat treatment and post-processing on microstructural evolution
subsections.content:
Post-processing is particularly consequential in SLM magnesium alloys because the as-built state is highly supersaturated, chemically heterogeneous, and defect-rich. Thermal exposure during stress relief, annealing, or solution treatment can therefore drive rapid recovery of dislocation substructures, partial recrystallization of the melt-pool cellular matrix, and coarsening or dissolution of non-equilibrium intermetallic networks that formed under extreme cooling rates. More broadly, heat treatment in Mg alloys is known to alter precipitation state, grain boundary chemistry, and texture-dependent deformation response, so its effects in SLM material are often amplified by the initially refined and metastable microstructure ref [2], ref [1].

For rare-earth-containing compositions such as WE43, post-build heat treatment is commonly used to reduce residual stress while promoting redistribution of Y/Nd-rich solutes and evolution from as-built segregation patterns toward more equilibrium precipitate populations. Studies on additively manufactured WE43 indicate that subsequent thermal treatment can modify grain morphology and second-phase distribution, with implications for both strength and corrosion behavior; in parallel, deformation-based post-processing routes such as hot isostatic pressing or severe plastic deformation can further close internal porosity and reconfigure texture through recrystallization-assisted grain refinement ref [11], ref [26].

The net microstructural outcome is therefore a balance between homogenization and over-aging. While moderate post-processing may stabilize the microstructure and improve ductility by relieving residual stress concentrations and reducing melt-pool-scale heterogeneity, excessive thermal exposure can coarsen strengthening precipitates, reduce the benefit of rapid-solidification grain refinement, and diminish the distinct nonequilibrium features that initially differentiate SLM magnesium from conventionally processed counterparts ref [2], ref [11].

subsections.section_title: Mechanical, Corrosion, and Functional Properties of SLM-Fabricated Magnesium Components
subsections.subsection_title: Density, dimensional accuracy, and surface integrity
subsections.content:
For SLM-fabricated magnesium components, density is primarily limited by the narrow processing window imposed by low boiling temperature, high vapor pressure, and oxidation sensitivity. Relative density generally improves when volumetric energy density is sufficient to suppress lack-of-fusion porosity, but excessive laser input can destabilize the melt track, intensify evaporation, and generate keyhole-type pores or spatter-induced defects. Reviews of laser processing of Mg alloys consistently emphasize that near-full densification is achievable only within a tightly controlled balance among laser power, scan speed, hatch spacing, layer thickness, and shielding conditions ref [12], ref [4].

Dimensional accuracy is likewise strongly coupled to thermal history. Rapid solidification and steep thermal gradients promote distortion, edge overgrowth, balling, and scan-track discontinuity, while Mg evaporation can alter local melt-pool volume and produce contour irregularity. In practice, dimensional deviations are often more severe in thin walls and overhang-like features, where heat accumulation and insufficient support exacerbate warping. Process optimization therefore requires not only densification-oriented parameter selection but also attention to scan strategy and powder characteristics, since particle size distribution and flowability affect layer uniformity and the reproducibility of part geometry ref [4], ref [16].

Surface integrity remains a persistent challenge for SLM magnesium. Typical as-built surfaces exhibit partially melted particles, adhered spatters, stair-stepping, and open surface-connected porosity, all of which raise roughness and can act as initiation sites for corrosion and fatigue damage. Because surface-connected defects are especially detrimental in biodegradable or load-bearing Mg components, post-processing such as machining, polishing, or chemical treatment is often necessary to decouple the beneficial bulk microstructure from the unfavorable as-built surface state ref [12], ref [5].

subsections.section_title: Mechanical, Corrosion, and Functional Properties of SLM-Fabricated Magnesium Components
subsections.subsection_title: Strength, ductility, hardness, and fracture behavior
subsections.content:
The tensile and hardness response of SLM-fabricated magnesium is governed primarily by the competition between rapid-solidification strengthening and defect-controlled embrittlement. Fine cellular or equiaxed microstructures, supersaturation, and refined second-phase distributions can raise yield strength and hardness relative to cast counterparts, but the attainable ductility remains highly sensitive to lack-of-fusion pores, entrapped gas, and solidification cracking. In WE43 processed by selective laser melting, high strengths were associated with substantial grain refinement and rare-earth-containing phases formed under rapid cooling, although elongation deteriorated when process-induced defects persisted ref [11]. Similar behavior has been reported for SLM Mg–9Al, where refined microstructures increased hardness and strength, but tensile scatter reflected porosity and incomplete fusion ref [6].

Fracture behavior therefore commonly reflects a mixed microstructure/defect control. Dense specimens tend to show predominantly transgranular quasi-cleavage with limited plastic deformation, consistent with the intrinsic HCP slip constraints of Mg and the strong textures that can arise during layerwise solidification. By contrast, specimens containing unfused regions or oxide-decorated boundaries often fail prematurely from stress concentration sites, with fracture surfaces showing cleavage facets, tear ridges, and pore-linked crack coalescence ref [1,2]. For pure Mg produced by SLM, the best mechanical performance has similarly been achieved only within a narrow processing window that suppresses balling and porosity; outside this window, strength and especially elongation decline rapidly despite fine grain size ref [17].

Overall, strengthening in SLM magnesium components is relatively accessible, whereas simultaneous retention of ductility and damage tolerance is more challenging. This makes fracture resistance a sensitive indicator of process stability, post-processing effectiveness, and texture control, rather than of microstructural refinement alone.

subsections.section_title: Mechanical, Corrosion, and Functional Properties of SLM-Fabricated Magnesium Components
subsections.subsection_title: Fatigue and cyclic durability
subsections.content:
Fatigue and cyclic durability remain comparatively underexplored for SLM-fabricated magnesium relative to monotonic strength, yet they are likely to be governed by the same defect-sensitive mechanisms established for additively manufactured metals more broadly. In laser powder bed fusion, lack-of-fusion pores, gas porosity, surface-connected defects, and tensile residual stresses act as dominant crack-initiation sites and can sharply reduce high-cycle fatigue strength even when static properties appear acceptable. This general defect-controlled framework has been emphasized in broader analyses of additive-manufacturing fatigue and residual stress, and is directly relevant to magnesium because of its limited room-temperature slip and pronounced notch sensitivity under cyclic loading ref [29], ref [24].

For SLM magnesium alloys, cyclic durability is therefore expected to depend strongly on volumetric density, contour quality, and post-processing. Fine cellular or rapidly solidified microstructures may raise yield strength, but fatigue resistance does not necessarily improve unless defect populations and roughness are simultaneously minimized. This trade-off is especially important for thin-walled or lattice biomedical components, where as-built surfaces and partially fused particles can create severe local stress concentrations. Reviews focused on magnesium additive manufacturing have accordingly identified fatigue data as a major knowledge gap and highlighted hot isostatic pressing, machining/polishing, and stress-relief treatments as probable routes to improve endurance performance ref [12], ref [9].

In practice, fatigue assessment of SLM magnesium should be coupled with corrosion-fatigue considerations, because cyclic loading in physiological or humid environments can accelerate crack initiation at surface films, corrosion pits, or subsurface pores. Consequently, reliable design will require integrated control of process-induced defects, residual stress, texture, and environmental degradation rather than optimization of tensile strength alone.

subsections.section_title: Mechanical, Corrosion, and Functional Properties of SLM-Fabricated Magnesium Components
subsections.subsection_title: Wear and tribological behavior
subsections.content:
Wear and tribological performance has been much less studied for SLM-fabricated magnesium than tensile strength or corrosion, but it is nevertheless important for lightweight moving components and temporary biomedical devices subjected to micromotion. In magnesium alloys generally, tribological response is governed by the competition between plastic smearing of the soft matrix, delamination, oxidative wear, and the load-bearing role of intermetallic phases; thus, SLM-induced grain refinement, solute supersaturation, and defect populations are all expected to shift wear behavior by modifying hardness, oxide stability, and crack-initiation susceptibility under sliding ref [1], ref [2].

For SLM Mg alloys, the fine cellular or rapidly solidified microstructures usually imply higher hardness than cast counterparts, which can reduce adhesive wear and ploughing at low to moderate loads. However, this potential benefit is conditional on defect control: lack-of-fusion pores, entrapped oxides, and rough as-built surfaces can act as third-body debris sources and accelerate subsurface crack formation. Because magnesium has limited intrinsic wear resistance, post-processing routes that simultaneously densify the part and smooth the surface are likely to be more influential for tribological reliability than bulk strength improvements alone.

A further complication is the strong coupling between wear and environment. In humid or physiological media, mechanically disrupted surface films can repeatedly rupture and reform, so tribocorrosion rather than pure dry sliding may dominate material loss. Reviews of magnesium biomaterials and corrosion consistently note that protective surface layers on Mg are unstable in chloride-containing solutions; under sliding contact, this instability can intensify both wear debris generation and localized degradation, making tribological assessment essential for realistic service evaluation of SLM Mg implants ref [15], ref [3].

subsections.section_title: Mechanical, Corrosion, and Functional Properties of SLM-Fabricated Magnesium Components
subsections.subsection_title: Corrosion and biodegradation performance
subsections.content:
Corrosion behavior is a central concern for SLM-fabricated magnesium because the process simultaneously refines microstructure and introduces heterogeneities that can accelerate localized attack. Rapid solidification often produces fine grains and a more homogeneous distribution of secondary phases, which can promote formation of comparatively uniform corrosion films; however, lack-of-fusion defects, keyhole porosity, partially melted particles, and evaporation-induced compositional fluctuations create micro-galvanic sites and crevice-like geometries that destabilize degradation in chloride-containing media. This dual effect is particularly important for biodegradable implants, where both the average dissolution rate and its spatial uniformity determine mechanical retention and tissue response.

Studies on additively manufactured biodegradable metals have therefore emphasized that corrosion performance cannot be inferred from density alone, but must be linked to pore morphology, surface condition, and post-processing history ref [10], ref [5]. For magnesium alloys such as WE43, the corrosion response is also strongly influenced by SLM-induced segregation of rare-earth-containing phases and by the as-built rough surface, which increases true exposed area and favors early pit initiation; polishing, hot isostatic pressing, or suitable heat treatment can reduce these effects, although excessive coarsening of second phases may be detrimental ref [11]. In physiological environments, the resulting biodegradation behavior further controls hydrogen evolution, alkalization, and ion release, all of which feed back into cytocompatibility and osseointegration ref [30].

Accordingly, assessment of SLM magnesium should combine immersion, electrochemical, and long-term biodegradation tests with microstructural characterization across multiple length scales. A key structure-property principle is that dense parts with controlled chemistry and minimized surface-connected defects tend to show slower and more uniform corrosion, whereas defect-rich as-built surfaces commonly exhibit accelerated and spatially heterogeneous degradation.

subsections.section_title: Mechanical, Corrosion, and Functional Properties of SLM-Fabricated Magnesium Components
subsections.subsection_title: Biocompatibility and biofunctionality
subsections.content:
For SLM-fabricated magnesium components, biocompatibility is governed less by the nominal alloy chemistry alone than by the local corrosion response created by the printed microstructure and surface state. Magnesium is intrinsically attractive for temporary implants because it is biodegradable and its elastic modulus is closer to that of bone than that of permanent metallic biomaterials; however, excessive degradation can generate rapid alkalization, hydrogen evolution, and local particle release, all of which influence cell attachment and tissue tolerance ref [3], ref [30]. In this context, the rough surfaces, partially fused particles, and compositional heterogeneities typical of as-built SLM parts can either support osteoblast anchorage or, if they accelerate localized corrosion, undermine cytocompatibility.

Biofunctionality therefore depends on balancing degradation-mediated biological stimulation with structural persistence. Rare-earth-containing Mg alloys such as WE43 have received particular attention because they combine printability with mechanical integrity, and porous or lattice architectures enabled by additive manufacturing can further promote bone ingrowth and mass transport when degradation is sufficiently controlled ref [5]. More broadly, the biological performance of biodegradable metals is highly application specific: orthopedic uses benefit from osteoconductive topography and gradual load transfer, whereas cardiovascular devices require far tighter control of corrosion rate, endothelial compatibility, and thrombogenicity ref [10].

For SLM Mg, this implies that post-processing is often as important as the build itself. Surface finishing, heat treatment, and bioactive or corrosion-mitigating coatings are commonly needed to reduce defect-assisted dissolution and to decouple favorable cell responses from the otherwise unstable as-built surface. Consequently, assessment of biocompatibility in printed Mg should be framed as a structure-corrosion-biology problem rather than a purely compositional one.

subsections.section_title: Mechanical, Corrosion, and Functional Properties of SLM-Fabricated Magnesium Components
subsections.subsection_title: Structure-property relationships
subsections.content:
In SLM-fabricated magnesium, structure–property relationships are governed by the unusually rapid solidification and cyclic reheating inherent to the process. These conditions commonly produce fine cellular or equiaxed grains, supersaturated solid solutions, and non-equilibrium second-phase distributions, which can increase yield strength and hardness relative to cast counterparts through grain refinement and solute strengthening. At the same time, the resulting anisotropy depends on the solidification texture, which is especially important in hcp Mg because deformation mode activation is highly orientation-sensitive ref [27], ref [28].

Defect populations introduced during SLM often dominate the transition from intrinsic microstructure-controlled behavior to defect-controlled performance. Lack-of-fusion pores, keyhole porosity, unmelted particles, and solidification cracking act as local stress concentrators that reduce tensile ductility and fatigue resistance, while residual stresses further promote crack initiation. Consequently, the beneficial effects of refined microstructure can only be realized when volumetric energy input and scan strategy suppress these defects without causing excessive evaporation or compositional instability ref [24].

The same structural features also control environmental performance. Grain refinement and rapid-solidification-induced phase redistribution may improve micro-galvanic uniformity, but porosity, surface-connected defects, and segregation can accelerate localized corrosion and biodegradation. For biomedical Mg alloys such as WE43, this means that process optimization must target a coupled property space in which texture, grain size, precipitate state, and defect density are simultaneously managed to balance strength, degradation rate, and biological reliability ref [11].

subsections.section_title: Applications, Post-Processing Strategies, and Future Research Directions
subsections.subsection_title: Biomedical applications of additively manufactured magnesium
subsections.content:
Biomedical interest in additively manufactured magnesium is driven by the combination of low density, elastic modulus closer to that of bone than traditional implant metals, and intrinsic biodegradability. These attributes are especially attractive for temporary orthopedic fixation and porous scaffolds, where gradual loss of mechanical support can be synchronized with tissue healing, potentially reducing stress shielding and eliminating secondary removal surgery. Broad reviews of magnesium biomaterials and biodegradable metals for AM have identified patient-specific geometry, controlled porosity, and locally tailored degradation as key advantages of powder-bed-based processing for this application space ref [3], ref [5].

For orthopedic use, lattice and trabecular architectures produced by selective laser melting or related routes offer a route to promote osseointegration while reducing stiffness and mass. However, the central biomedical challenge is not simply manufacturability, but balancing early-stage mechanical integrity with corrosion kinetics, gas evolution, and biocompatibility of alloying elements and corrosion products. In this regard, rare-earth-containing systems such as WE43 have attracted attention because they are among the few AM magnesium alloys to show a usable processing window and comparatively strong as-built properties, although their long-term biological assessment remains application-specific and more complex than that of high-purity Mg-based systems ref [10].

For cardiovascular and other miniaturized temporary devices, the design logic differs: thin struts, predictable radial support, and tightly controlled degradation become paramount. Reviews on biodegradable metallic stents have highlighted magnesium as a leading candidate, but also emphasize that localized corrosion, mechanical reliability under cyclic loading, and surface-state control are decisive barriers to translation ref [30]. Consequently, biomedical deployment of additively manufactured magnesium will likely depend on integrated alloy design, architected geometry, and post-processing strategies that tune both interfacial bioresponse and time-dependent corrosion-mechanical performance.

subsections.section_title: Applications, Post-Processing Strategies, and Future Research Directions
subsections.subsection_title: Lightweight structural and functional applications
subsections.content:
Beyond biomedical use, SLM magnesium is attractive for lightweight structural and functional components where low density, high specific stiffness, and electromagnetic or vibration-related functionality are valued. Classical assessments of magnesium alloys as structural materials already identify transportation, aerospace, and portable-device housings as application spaces in which mass reduction can translate directly into fuel, payload, or ergonomic benefits ref [1]. In this context, additive manufacturing is especially relevant not because it simply reproduces wrought magnesium parts, but because it enables geometry-driven performance gains through part consolidation, local reinforcement, and integrated thermal or energy-absorbing features.

The main opportunity is therefore in low-to-moderate load components whose value derives from specific performance rather than absolute strength. Reviews of high-strength magnesium alloy development show that alloy design in Mg is constrained by hexagonal crystal plasticity, temperature sensitivity, and corrosion-environment interactions ref [2]; these same constraints imply that SLM magnesium will likely find earlier adoption in brackets, housings, UAV components, sacrificial lightweight fixtures, and thermally responsive enclosures rather than in highly fatigue-critical primary structures. At the same time, the process can generate fine microstructures and non-equilibrium phase distributions, offering pathways to tune stiffness-to-weight ratio, damping response, and potentially functional behavior if microstructure and defect populations are tightly controlled ref [6].

For broader deployment, property qualification must move from coupon-level tensile metrics to application-relevant datasets including fatigue, crash/impact energy absorption, environmental durability, and dimensional stability under service heating. This is consistent with broader assessments of additive magnesium, which emphasize that the practical niche of SLM Mg will depend on linking process windows and post-processing to component-specific performance envelopes rather than pursuing strength alone ref [9].

subsections.section_title: Applications, Post-Processing Strategies, and Future Research Directions
subsections.subsection_title: Lattice structures, topology optimization, and multifunctional design
subsections.content:
Lattice architectures are especially attractive for SLM magnesium because they exploit the alloy system’s low density while introducing an additional design variable—porosity—that can be tuned for stiffness, energy absorption, transport, and biological response. In magnesium, this is particularly relevant for degradable implants, where open-cell geometries can reduce the apparent modulus toward that of bone and increase surface area for tissue interaction, but they also accelerate corrosion and magnify the importance of local defects at struts and nodes. This creates a coupled design problem in which architecture, process window, and degradation behavior must be optimized simultaneously rather than sequentially ref [10], ref [5].

Topology optimization therefore offers a natural framework for magnesium LPBF/SLM, enabling mass-efficient load paths and patient- or component-specific geometries that are not accessible to conventional processing. However, optimization strategies developed for inert, nondegrading metals are not directly transferable: for magnesium, constraints must incorporate printability, anisotropic mechanical response, corrosion allowance, and property evolution with time in service. For biodegradable scaffolds and fixation devices, the target is often not maximum static strength alone, but controlled loss of mechanical support synchronized with tissue healing, which motivates functionally graded porosity and spatially heterogeneous architectures ref [10], ref [31].

A broader multifunctional design perspective is also emerging. Beyond lightweighting, magnesium lattices could integrate osseointegration, mass transport, vibration damping, and tailored collapse behavior in a single component. Realizing this vision will require tighter coupling between computational design, process simulation, and in vitro/in vivo validation, as emphasized more generally in additive manufacturing research on topology optimization and architected materials ref [31], ref [32].

subsections.section_title: Applications, Post-Processing Strategies, and Future Research Directions
subsections.subsection_title: Post-processing for performance enhancement
subsections.content:
Post-processing is often indispensable for selective laser melted magnesium because as-built parts can retain high residual stresses, process-induced porosity, rough surfaces, and nonequilibrium microstructures that limit fatigue strength, corrosion resistance, and dimensional reliability. Stress-relief and homogenization treatments are therefore attractive first-line interventions: they can reduce stored strain energy and stabilize microstructural heterogeneity, although care is required to avoid excessive grain coarsening or precipitate dissolution that would compromise strength in age-hardenable Mg alloys. The broader rationale for thermal post-processing in additively manufactured metals is well established in the residual-stress literature, and the exceptional sensitivity of magnesium alloys to texture and phase constitution makes these treatments especially consequential ref [24], ref [27].

For biomedical and lightweight structural components, surface-focused post-processing may be even more critical than bulk heat treatment. Machining, abrasive finishing, laser remelting, shot peening, and coating deposition can all reduce effective stress concentrators and alter near-surface reactivity, thereby improving both fatigue performance and corrosion behavior. In biodegradable magnesium, this is particularly important because rough, partially sintered surface features can accelerate localized degradation; conversely, carefully designed coatings or anodized/conversion layers may delay early corrosion while preserving the long-term resorbability required for implants ref [3].

A promising direction is the development of integrated post-processing routes tailored to alloy chemistry and application, for example combining hot isostatic pressing or thermal treatment with surface densification and biofunctional or protective coatings. For conventional AM alloys, such combined routes have already shown strong benefits for defect closure and fatigue enhancement, suggesting a useful template for SLM magnesium provided oxidation, vaporization-related chemistry changes, and corrosion-sensitive microstructures are simultaneously controlled ref [29].

subsections.section_title: Applications, Post-Processing Strategies, and Future Research Directions
subsections.subsection_title: Qualification, standardization, and scalability
subsections.content:
Qualification of SLM magnesium components remains more difficult than for mature alloys because build quality is strongly coupled to oxidation, evaporation loss, pore formation, and narrow processing windows. As a result, qualification cannot rely solely on nominal machine settings; it must integrate feedstock control, atmosphere management, traceable parameter sets, and part-specific verification of density, chemistry, surface condition, and defect population. More broadly, process qualification frameworks developed for metal additive manufacturing increasingly emphasize in situ sensing, data fusion, and closed-loop control as prerequisites for robust certification, especially when alloy-specific instability is expected ref [22], ref [20].

Standardization is still at an early stage for additively manufactured magnesium. Existing AM standards provide general terminology, test philosophies, and quality-management structures, but magnesium-specific acceptance criteria for powder reuse, oxygen pickup, flammability mitigation, corrosion-sensitive surface states, and biodegradation performance are not yet harmonized. For biomedical uses, qualification must also bridge conventional AM metrics with implant-specific evidence on degradation behavior, cytocompatibility, and sterilization compatibility, highlighting the need for dedicated consensus standards and interlaboratory benchmarking ref [5].

Scalability will depend on translating laboratory parameter maps into statistically reproducible manufacturing routes across machines, build sizes, and powder lots. This requires digital process records, robust monitoring of melt-pool signatures, and predictive models linking process signatures to defect formation and final properties ref [20], ref [23]. For magnesium, scalable production is therefore inseparable from qualification science: without standardized powder handling, safety protocols, and machine-to-machine comparability, industrial and clinical deployment will remain limited.

subsections.section_title: Applications, Post-Processing Strategies, and Future Research Directions
subsections.subsection_title: Sustainability, safety, and economic considerations
subsections.content:
From a sustainability perspective, SLM magnesium offers a mixed picture. Near-net-shape fabrication can reduce buy-to-fly ratios and machining scrap, which is attractive for both biomedical and lightweight applications, but the environmental benefit is moderated by the high energy intensity of laser powder bed fusion and by powder losses associated with oxidation, spatter, and limited recyclability. More generally, powder reuse in laser powder bed fusion can alter particle size distribution, flowability, chemistry, and defect susceptibility, making closed-loop powder management an important lever for both resource efficiency and quality assurance ref [16].

Safety considerations are unusually prominent for magnesium because fine powders are highly reactive. Reviews on magnesium oxidation and on ignition/combustion of magnesium powders show that particle size, oxide condition, moisture, and thermal history strongly influence flammability, underscoring the need for rigorous inert-gas control, powder handling protocols, and explosion-mitigation strategies across storage, sieving, and build-chamber operations ref [14], ref [13]. For clinical products, safety also extends to residue control, sterilization compatibility, and corrosion by-products, which can impose additional process and validation costs.

Economically, broader adoption depends on balancing the premium cost of inert processing, powder qualification, and post-processing against value delivered through mass reduction, patient-specific geometries, or accelerated design cycles. Qualification costs remain especially significant because magnesium systems often require tighter control of atmosphere, feedstock condition, and defect populations than more established alloys. Thus, scalable deployment will likely rely on integrated techno-economic frameworks that couple powder lifecycle management, safe factory operation, and application-specific certification pathways rather than considering cost, safety, and sustainability in isolation.

subsections.section_title: Applications, Post-Processing Strategies, and Future Research Directions
subsections.subsection_title: Emerging opportunities and open research questions
subsections.content:
Emerging opportunities in SLM magnesium lie in moving from proof-of-concept specimens toward application-specific, functionally graded, and data-enabled components. A particularly important research direction is the coupling of geometry, alloy chemistry, and degradation design so that mechanical support, corrosion kinetics, and tissue or fluid interaction can be co-optimized rather than treated sequentially. This need is especially acute for biodegradable devices, where additive manufacturing offers unique control over porous architectures but also introduces unresolved questions regarding local chemistry, defect populations, and their influence on in vivo performance ref [5], ref [30].

At the process level, major open questions concern how rapid solidification, evaporation, oxidation, and thermal cycling jointly determine solute redistribution, texture development, crack susceptibility, and build-to-build variability in magnesium alloys. More predictive multiscale modeling frameworks are needed to connect melt-pool phenomena with mesoscale defect formation and component-scale properties, while sensing and closed-loop control remain underdeveloped for highly reactive Mg powders ref [23], ref [22]. These issues are not merely scientific; they directly affect qualification pathways and the feasibility of robust industrial deployment.

A further opportunity is the accelerated discovery of AM-specific magnesium alloys and post-processing routes tailored for the non-equilibrium conditions of laser processing. Instead of adapting conventional wrought or cast compositions, future work should target compositions with wider processing windows, reduced hot tearing tendency, and controllable biodegradation or fatigue resistance. Progress will likely come from integrating alloy design, process monitoring, and application-led testing under realistic service environments rather than relying on room-temperature coupon data alone ref [30], ref [23].
